​
      Know-Ta!: A Dual-Branch Deep Learning Framework for

    Cross-Platform AI-Generated Music Detection with Bayesian

                      Uncertainty Estimation





                A Computer Science Research Title Proposal
​


                 Presented to the College of Information and Computing ​
                      University of Southeastern Philippines, Davao City​
                               Bo. Obrero, Davao City
​


                                                                           ​
                           In Partial Fulfillment of the Requirements for ​
                       Computer Science Research Methods​
                                                                           ​



                              Delgado, Kent Paulo R.

                                                                             ​
                                                                             ​

                                 March 8, 2026

Chapter 1: The Problem and Its Background
Background of the Study
       Musical composition has always been a deeply human endeavor, one that draws from
emotion, lived experience, and creative intent [1]. However, the rapid integration of Artificial
Intelligence  into music production has fundamentally transformed how music  is created,
distributed, and consumed [2]. AI-powered systems can now analyze massive collections of
existing songs to learn complex patterns in melody, rhythm, harmony, and style, enabling them
to generate original compositions at an unprecedented scale and speed [3]. Tools such as Suno
and Udio exemplify this capability, leveraging Transformer and Diffusion model architectures to
produce complete songs with vocals, lyrics, and instrumentation across multiple genres [11].
Platforms  like ChatMusician  further demonstrate  that Large Language Models can now
compose music directly from text descriptions [10], while generative architectures including
Variational Autoencoders (VAEs), Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs), and Diffusion
Models continue to push the boundaries of synthetic music realism [4][9]. What was once a
creative process rooted exclusively in human artistry has now become a domain increasingly
shared and contested with machine intelligence.
      The consequences of this  shift are measurable and urgent. A study conducted by
Deezer and  Ipsos  found  that 97%  of  participants were unable  to  distinguish between
human-made and fully AI-generated music [12], demonstrating that human perception alone is
no longer a reliable safeguard against synthetic content. This perceptual indistinguishability has
allowed AI-generated tracks to flood streaming platforms at scale, directly threatening the
livelihoods of human musicians. Projections estimate a $12.7 billion loss for musicians by 2028
[13], with creators facing a 27% projected revenue drop within the same period [14]. These
figures underscore a critical reality: without reliable detection technology, the music ecosystem
cannot protect the authenticity of human-made work or ensure fair compensation for the artists
who create it.
       Existing detection approaches have attempted to address this problem but remain
technically insufficient. Traditional machine learning methods such as Support Vector Machines
and Random  Forests  provide  interpretable  baselines  for  audio  classification  [5],  while
Convolutional Neural Networks extract spectral features from audio representations [6] and
Recurrent Neural Networks capture temporal inconsistencies in AI-generated sequences [7].
Advanced systems further leverage attention mechanisms  in Transformer architectures to
capture complex long-range musical patterns and compositional structure [8]. Despite these
efforts, the state of AI music detection is critically limited by three fundamental failures. First, the
most advanced published music  detector, which achieves 99.8% accuracy  in  controlled
conditions, completely collapses when subjected to basic audio transformations such as pitch
shifts or codec re-encoding, defaulting to labeling  all tracks as real when platform-specific
artifacts are obscured [22]. Second, detection models trained on one AI platform consistently fail
to generalize to music generated by platforms unseen during training, meaning that every new
AI tool released renders existing detectors partially obsolete [24]. Third, and most critically,
every  existing music  detection system processes the  full blended audio  signal  without
separating vocal and instrumental components, and no current system incorporates human

biological vocal features despite their established value as biomarkers of authentic human
performance  [23]. A comprehensive benchmark  of  detection methods  explicitly  identified
multimodal detection as the most urgent and unaddressed direction in the field [23]. This study
is a direct technical response to that open call.
      The urgency of this problem extends beyond the global music industry and is acutely felt
in the Philippines. The Intellectual Property Office of the Philippines (IPOPHL) currently does not
register AI-generated content for copyright, leaving both human artists and AI developers in a
legally ambiguous space [15]. As synthetic tracks from platforms like Suno and Udio continue to
flood streaming charts, Filipino artists face intensifying competition from content that can be
produced instantly and at virtually no cost [16]. This challenge is compounded by the fact that in
2024, musical compositions accounted for only 7% of the 6,552 copyright certificates issued in
the Philippines [17], indicating that a significant portion of local music remains unregistered and
therefore more vulnerable to unauthorized AI replication.
       At the local level, Davao City reflects these national challenges while facing additional
constraints rooted in limited research infrastructure. Although the city has made strides toward
becoming a technology hub in Mindanao through initiatives such as innovation summits [18],
local musicians continue to operate without the protection of a strong regulatory framework for
AI-generated content. The absence of city-specific research on AI music's impact on Davao's
creative community means that local artists, policymakers, and music organizations lack the
data necessary to make informed decisions about protecting homegrown musical works.
            It is within this context that the researcher proposes Know-Ta!, a Dual-Branch Deep
Learning  Framework  for  Cross-Platform  AI-Generated  Music  Detection  with  Bayesian
Uncertainty Estimation. The system processes English-language music tracks by first separating
audio stems using the Demucs source separation model [19], then independently analyzing
spectral features through an EfficientNet-B0 Audio Branch [20] and vocal prosodic features
through a Bidirectional LSTM Vocal Branch  [7]. The two branches are fused through an
attention-based mechanism that dynamically weights each branch's contribution based on the
input content, and Monte Carlo Dropout is applied to produce calibrated Bayesian confidence
scores that communicate the system's certainty on a per-track and per-branch basis. By
combining stem separation, dual-branch analysis, and uncertainty quantification, Know-Ta! is
proposed as the first music detection system to simultaneously address the generalization gap,
the blended-signal limitation, and the absence of biological vocal feature analysis that current
detection research has left unresolved.
Statement of the Problem
       This study seeks to develop and evaluate Know-Ta!, a dual-branch deep learning
framework designed to accurately and transparently distinguish human-made from AI-generated
English-language music across previously unseen AI generation platforms. Specifically, this
study seeks to answer the following questions:
    ●​ Can Know-Ta! accurately tell the difference between a song made by a human and a
      song generated by Artificial Intelligence?
    ●​ Does analyzing the audio and the voice of a song separately produce better detection
        results than analyzing the full mixed track as a single input?
    ●​ How well does Know-Ta! perform when tested on AI-generated music from platforms it
      has never encountered during training?

●​  In cases where the audio and vocal analysis produce conflicting results, how effectively
      does the Bayesian uncertainty component communicate the system's level of confidence
        to the user?
Significance of the Study
      The authenticity and originality of music is becoming an alarming issue in the digital age,
especially as AI music generation tools grow increasingly accessible and indistinguishable from
human-made work. The outcomes of this study have the capacity to address these challenges
and create meaningful impact across the music industry, deep learning research, and digital
content platforms. By combining stem separation, dual-branch spectral and prosodic analysis,
attention-based fusion, and Bayesian uncertainty estimation, the findings of this research
contribute to the improvement of AI content detection accuracy, cross-platform generalization,
and transparency in music authenticity verification.
Music Platforms and Content Moderators
      Through the use of a dual-branch architecture that independently analyzes audio
spectral  features and  vocal  prosodic  characteristics before combining them through an
attention-based fusion mechanism, this research provides music platforms, content moderators,
and listeners with a detection tool that generalizes across multiple AI generation platforms
rather than memorizing the artifacts of a single source. The inclusion of per-branch confidence
scoring means the system can surface nuanced verdicts, such as cases where instrumental
features suggest AI generation but vocal characteristics suggest human performance, giving
content moderators a more complete and actionable picture than a binary label alone can
provide. The cross-platform performance drop metric introduced in this study provides the field
with a standardized way to measure and report generalization failure, a contribution that no prior
music detection paper has made explicitly.
Deep Learning Researchers
      The results of this study offer AI researchers practical insights into how dual-branch
architectures perform in audio classification tasks, particularly in detecting synthetic content
across unseen platforms. The integration of Monte Carlo Dropout-based Bayesian uncertainty
estimation  into a  dual-branch music  detection framework  is a  novel  combination  that
demonstrates how calibrated confidence reporting can be added to existing deep learning
architectures  without  requiring fundamental  redesign. By documenting the strengths and
limitations of this approach through a structured six-model ablation study, this research provides
a replicable methodological blueprint for future work on detecting AI-generated content in other
media domains including speech, podcasts, and video.
Independent Artists and Music Listeners
      Music listeners, independent artists, and platforms with limited resources for content
verification are the primary beneficiaries of Know-Ta!. The system  is deployed as a web
application that allows any user to upload an English-language music  file and receive a
real-time authenticity verdict, per-branch confidence scores, a Bayesian uncertainty report, and
a  plain-language  explanation  of the detected  indicators,  without  requiring any  technical
expertise  or  specialized  software. This  directly addresses the  accessibility gap  in music
authentication: professional verification services are not available to most independent artists,
particularly in developing music markets.
Filipino Artists and Local Policymakers

In the Philippine setting, where the Intellectual Property Office does not yet register
AI-generated content for copyright [15] and musical compositions represent only a small fraction
of copyright certificates issued annually [17], Know-Ta! offers Filipino artists, including those
based in Davao City, an accessible means of verifying the authenticity of their own work and
identifying potential unauthorized AI replication. By making transparent and interpretable music
authenticity  verification  freely  accessible, Know-Ta! empowers  artists,  listeners, and  local
policymakers alike to make informed decisions about the music they create, consume, and
protect.
Future Researchers
       This study may serve as a reference  for future researchers who wish to explore
dual-branch or multimodal architectures, Bayesian uncertainty estimation, or cross-platform
generalization in the broader domain of synthetic media detection, including speech, video, and
image forensics.
Scope and Delimitation
       This study  is  limited  to the design, development, and evaluation of Know-Ta!, a
dual-branch deep learning detection system for English-language music tracks. The system is
trained and internally tested using the SONICS dataset [46], which contains tracks sourced from
Suno and Udio, and is evaluated for cross-platform generalization using the AIME dataset,
which contains tracks sourced from twelve AI platforms not encountered during  training.
Because both datasets consist exclusively of English-language music, the detection capability of
Know-Ta! is confined to English-language tracks; the system's performance on music in other
languages, including Filipino and other regional languages, is not evaluated in this study and is
identified as a direction for future work.
The system architecture  is delimited to two analytical branches, an Audio Branch built on
EfficientNet-B0 that processes Mel-Spectrogram representations of the instrumental stem, and a
Vocal Branch built on Bidirectional LSTM that processes prosodic features extracted from the
isolated vocal stem produced by the Demucs source separation model [19]. The study does not
explore   alternative  backbone  architectures  such  as  ResNet,  VGG,  DenseNet,  or
Transformer-based audio encoders beyond their inclusion as points of comparison drawn from
cited literature; EfficientNet-B0 and Bi-LSTM are adopted as the primary branch architectures
based on prior benchmark evidence [25][28]. Uncertainty estimation is delimited to Monte Carlo
Dropout with Temperature Scaling calibration; alternative approaches such as Deep Ensembles
[42] are acknowledged as a stronger but more computationally expensive alternative and are
explicitly reserved for future work rather than implemented in this study.
Evaluation  is delimited to the six metrics defined in this study, namely Accuracy, Precision,
Recall, F1-Score, ROC-AUC, and Cross-Platform Performance Drop Percentage, computed on
the SONICS internal test partition and the AIME cross-platform test set. The study does not
evaluate  real-time streaming  detection, does not address legal or copyright enforcement
mechanisms, and does not extend to non-English music, purely instrumental genres without any
vocal content beyond what is naturally present in the datasets used, or platforms other than
those represented in SONICS and AIME. The final system is delimited to deployment as a web
application accessible via file upload in MP3 or WAV format; mobile application deployment and
integration with third-party streaming platforms are outside the scope of this study.
Chapter 2: Review of Related Literature and Studies

Related Literature
       This chapter presents a review of related literature and studies that provide the technical
and theoretical foundation for Know-Ta!. The review is organized thematically, moving from the
emergence  of  AI-generated  music and  its  industry  impact,  through  existing  detection
approaches and their limitations, to the specific architectural components adopted in this study,
namely source separation, spectral and prosodic feature analysis, attention-based fusion, and
Bayesian uncertainty estimation.
The Emergence of AI-Generated Music
       Musical composition has traditionally been regarded as an expression of human emotion
and lived experience  [1], but the accessibility of AI-based composition tools has begun to
reshape the creative landscape for independent artists [2]. AI systems are now capable of
learning complex patterns in melody, rhythm, harmony, and style from large song collections
and  generating  original  compositions  at  scale  [3]. Recent surveys document the  rapid
advancement  of  generative  architectures  for  music,  including  Variational  Autoencoders,
Generative Adversarial Networks, and Diffusion Models [4][9]. Platforms such as Suno and Udio
apply Transformer and Diffusion architectures to generate complete songs, including vocals,
lyrics, and  instrumentation, across multiple genres  [11], while systems  like ChatMusician
demonstrate that Large Language Models can compose music directly from text prompts [10].
Computational intelligence techniques more broadly continue to expand the range of musical
tasks that can be automated [8].
Industry and Economic Impact
      The practical consequences of widespread AI music generation are already measurable.
A Deezer and Ipsos study found that 97% of listeners could not reliably distinguish AI-generated
tracks from human-made ones [12]. Industry projections estimate losses of $12.7 billion for
musicians by 2028 [13] and a 27% projected revenue drop for creators within the same period
[14], underscoring the economic urgency of reliable detection tools.
Legal and Regulatory Context in the Philippines
        Locally, the Intellectual Property Office of the Philippines does not currently register
AI-generated content  for copyright, leaving  artists and developers in a legally ambiguous
position [15]. Reports indicate that Filipino artists face growing competition from AI-generated
tracks that can be produced instantly and at minimal cost [16], compounded by the fact that
musical compositions accounted for only 7% of copyright certificates issued in the Philippines in
2024 [17]. At the regional level, Davao City's growing technology sector [18] has not yet been
matched by research or regulatory attention specific to AI-generated music's impact on the local
creative community.
Traditional and Early Deep Learning Detection Approaches
       Early approaches to audio classification relied on traditional machine learning methods.
Support Vector Machines have been applied to musical genre classification [5], and more recent
reviews position SVM- and Random Forest-based classifiers as an interpretable but limited first
phase  of  detection  research  [37].  Convolutional  Neural Network  architectures such as
AudioRepInceptionNext extract spectral features efficiently from audio representations [6], while
Recurrent Neural Networks and related sequence models capture temporal patterns relevant to
music generation and detection [7]. Transformer-based architectures with attention mechanisms
have further improved the modeling of long-range musical structure [8].

Limitations of Current AI Music Detection Systems
       Despite this progress, published detection systems exhibit critical weaknesses. Afchar,
Meseguer-Brocal, and Hennequin [22] report that a music detector achieving 99.8% accuracy
under controlled conditions collapses entirely when subjected to basic transformations such as
pitch shifting or codec re-encoding, defaulting to labeling all tracks as real once platform-specific
artifacts are removed. Sroka et al. [24] similarly demonstrate that detectors trained on one AI
platform generalize poorly to platforms unseen during training, meaning every new generative
tool erodes the reliability of existing detectors. Li et al. [23] provide the most direct motivation for
this study, presenting a comprehensive benchmark of detection methods that identifies two
unresolved  gaps:  the  reliance on blended  audio  signals  without  separating  vocal and
instrumental components, and the absence of biologically grounded human vocal features, such
as breathing pause  patterns and  vibrato  regularity, despite  their demonstrated value as
authenticity biomarkers. Their benchmark explicitly names multimodal detection as the most
urgent unaddressed direction in the field, a call to which this study directly responds.
Source Separation
      Défossez et al. [19] introduced Demucs, a waveform-domain source separation model
capable of isolating vocal and instrumental stems from a mixed audio signal. This capability
underlies the dual-branch design of Know-Ta!, allowing the Audio Branch and Vocal Branch to
receive clean, targeted inputs rather than a blended signal.
Spectral Feature Analysis and the Audio Branch
      Tan and Le [20] introduced EfficientNet, a family of Convolutional Neural Networks that
use compound  coefficient scaling to  jointly optimize network width, depth, and resolution,
achieving strong accuracy with comparatively few parameters relative to architectures such as
ResNet, VGG, and DenseNet. Choi et al. [21] demonstrate the effectiveness of self-supervised
pre-training for music classification tasks. A 2025 benchmark by Bajwa, Castiglione, and Pero
[25] directly compared EfficientNet-B0 against VGG16, VGG19, ResNet50, DenseNet121, and
MobileNetV2 on Mel-Spectrograms for audio deepfake detection and found EfficientNet-B0 to
be  the  strongest  performer,  motivating  its  selection  for the Audio Branch  of Know-Ta!.
Wolf-Monheim [26] further shows that Mel-Spectrogram representations outperform alternative
spectral representations, including MFCCs, CQT chromagrams, and cyclic tempograms, for
CNN-based audio  classification,  informing the choice of Mel-Spectrograms as the Audio
Branch's input representation.
Prosodic Feature Analysis and the Vocal Branch
       Leglaive, Hennequin, and Badeau  [27]  originally proposed  Bidirectional Recurrent
Neural Networks for singing voice detection, arguing that vocal characteristics such as vibrato
and breathing pauses require both past and future temporal context to be properly identified, a
requirement that unidirectional architectures cannot satisfy. Al-Hussaini et al. [28] compared
LSTM, Bidirectional LSTM, and Transformer architectures on audio deepfake detection and
found that Bi-LSTM achieved the best Equal Error Rate (0.43%) and highest overall accuracy
among the three. Muruganandham et al. [29], in a 2025 Nature-published study, confirm that
integrating prosodic features such as pitch, temporal dynamics, and glottal parameters into
parallel  LSTM-based  modules  significantly  improves  real-versus-fake  audio  separability
compared to spectral features alone. Li et al. [23] provide the theoretical grounding for the
specific prosodic features adopted in this study, demonstrating that the absence of regular

human vocal biomarkers, including breathing pause patterns, vibrato  regularity, and pitch
micro-variation, is a reliable and peer-reviewed signal for distinguishing authentic human audio
from machine-generated audio.
Attention Mechanisms and Multimodal Fusion
      Vaswani et al. [30] formally introduced the attention mechanism, enabling models to
learn which inputs deserve greater weight based on the content of the specific input being
processed. Ranipa, Zhu, and Swamy [32] show that simple concatenation-based early fusion
underperforms attention-based fusion because  it cannot suppress irrelevant information or
emphasize the most discriminative signal. Huang et al. [33] provide a theoretical foundation for
multimodal fusion, proving that the utility of adding a complementary modality is monotonically
non-decreasing, meaning that combining two branches capturing different aspects of the same
problem can only maintain or improve performance  relative to either branch alone. This
theoretical  result  is supported  empirically by Negroni  et  al.  [31], whose attention-based
mixture-of-experts approach ranked first globally across all tasks in the 2025 SAFE International
Audio Deepfake Detection Challenge.
Ablation Methodology
      Meyes et al. [34] establish the formal methodology for ablation studies in artificial neural
networks, arguing that the contribution of individual architectural components cannot be claimed
without removing them and measuring the resulting change in performance. Sheikholeslami et
al.  [35]  extend  this  methodology  to modern  machine  learning  pipelines. Yadav and
Mangalampalli [36] and Murty, Tomar, and Koolagudi [38] apply comparable ablation structures
in recent CNN-BiLSTM hybrid deepfake detection research, providing the comparative template
adopted for the six-model ablation study in this research.
Bayesian Uncertainty Estimation
      Gal and Ghahramani [39] demonstrate that dropout, when kept active during inference
and applied across multiple forward passes, functions as a practical approximation of Bayesian
inference in deep neural networks, a technique known as Monte Carlo Dropout. Kendall and Gal
[40] extend  this framework by distinguishing between aleatoric uncertainty, which reflects
ambiguity inherent in the input  itself, and epistemic uncertainty, which reflects gaps in the
model's training exposure, a distinction adopted directly in the design of Know-Ta!. Guo et al.
[41] show that raw neural network confidence scores are frequently poorly calibrated and
introduce  Temperature   Scaling  as  a   lightweight   post-training   calibration  method.
Lakshminarayanan, Pritzel, and Blundell [42] propose Deep Ensembles as a stronger, though
more  computationally  expensive,  alternative  for  uncertainty  estimation, which  this study
identifies as a direction for future work.
Evaluation Metrics and Benchmark Datasets
      Sujon  et  al. [43] provide empirical guidance on the appropriate use of Accuracy,
Precision, Recall, and F1-Score in predictive model evaluation. Chandra et al. [44], through the
Deepfake-Eval-2024  benchmark,  identify  selective  single-metric  reporting  as  a  critical
methodological flaw  in  prior detection literature and recommend standardized, multi-metric
evaluation  protocols.  Jugade  et   al.  [45]  further  support  the  use  of ROC-AUC  for
threshold-independent comparison across detection systems. Rahman et al. [46] introduce the
SONICS dataset, an ICLR 2025 benchmark of 97,164 English-language tracks used as the
primary training and internal testing data for this study, while the AIME dataset supplies an

independent,  non-overlapping  set  of  AI  platforms  used  exclusively  for  cross-platform
generalization testing.
Synthesis
      The reviewed literature establishes that AI-generated music has become perceptually
indistinguishable from human-made music [12], carries significant economic consequences for
musicians [13][14], and remains inadequately regulated, both globally and within the Philippine
context [15][17]. At the same time, the reviewed detection literature reveals three converging
and unresolved limitations: published detectors fail under simple audio transformations [22], fail
to generalize across AI platforms not seen during training [24], and uniformly neglect both the
separation of vocal and instrumental signals and the incorporation of biologically grounded
human vocal features [23]. Individually, the architectural components reviewed in this chapter,
namely Demucs-based source separation  [19],  EfficientNet-B0  spectral  analysis  [20][25],
Bi-LSTM prosodic analysis  [27][28][29], attention-based multimodal fusion [30][31][33], and
Monte  Carlo  Dropout-based  Bayesian  uncertainty  estimation  [39][40], have each been
independently validated in adjacent domains. However, no reviewed study combines all of these
components into a single framework applied specifically to cross-platform, dual-signal AI music
detection. This gap forms the basis for the design of Know-Ta!, which integrates these validated
components into a unified, dual-branch detection framework.
Theoretical Framework
       This study is anchored on three theoretical foundations that jointly justify the architectural
design of Know-Ta!.
Bayesian Approximation Theory
      Gal and Ghahramani's [39] theory of Dropout as a Bayesian Approximation establishes
that a neural network with dropout applied at inference time, sampled across multiple stochastic
forward passes, approximates a Bayesian posterior distribution over its predictions. Kendall and
Gal [40] extend this theory by formally separating aleatoric uncertainty (irreducible ambiguity in
the data) from epistemic uncertainty (reducible uncertainty from limited model exposure). This
theoretical foundation justifies Know-Ta!'s use of Monte Carlo Dropout to produce calibrated
confidence scores rather than a single deterministic prediction, directly addressing the risk of
overconfident false positives in a music authentication context.
Attention Theory
      Vaswani et al.'s [30] attention mechanism theory establishes that a model can learn to
assign dynamic, content-dependent weights to different inputs rather than treating all inputs as
equally important. This theory underlies the attention-based fusion layer of Know-Ta!, which
learns weighting parameters for the Audio Branch and Vocal Branch that adapt based on the
characteristics of each input track.
Multimodal Learning Theory
      Huang et al.'s [33] theory of multimodal learning provides a mathematical guarantee that
the  utility function for incorporating an additional, complementary modality is monotonically
non-decreasing. Applied to this study, this theorem guarantees that combining the Audio Branch
and Vocal Branch, which capture fundamentally different aspects of a music track, can only
maintain or improve detection performance relative to either branch operating independently,
provided the  fusion mechanism  is  properly designed. This theoretical guarantee  directly
motivates the dual-branch architecture at the core of Know-Ta!.

Conceptual Framework
      Guided by the theoretical foundations above, this study conceptualizes the detection
process as a three-stage pipeline consisting of Input, Process, and Output components,
illustrated in the methodological framework presented in Chapter 3 (Figure 1).
The Input component consists of raw, English-language audio tracks drawn from the SONICS
and AIME datasets, comprising both human-made and AI-generated music. The Process
component encompasses data preprocessing and stem separation using Demucs; independent
feature extraction of Mel-Spectrogram (audio) and prosodic (vocal) features; parallel modeling
through the EfficientNet-B0 Audio Branch and Bi-LSTM Vocal Branch; attention-based fusion of
the two branches' outputs; and the application of Monte Carlo Dropout to generate Bayesian
confidence  estimates. The Output component consists of the  final  classification (Real or
AI-Generated), the overall Bayesian Confidence Score, per-branch confidence scores for the
Audio and Vocal Branches, a conflict flag for diverging branch verdicts, and, ultimately, a
real-time authenticity report delivered through the deployed web application. This conceptual
structure ensures  that every design  decision, from source separation through Bayesian
calibration, is traceable to a specific gap identified in the reviewed literature.
Chapter 3: Research Methodology
Research Design
       This  study  employs  a  developmental and  experimental  research  design.   It  is
developmental in that  it involves the design, construction, and implementation of a novel deep
learning system, and it is experimental in that the resulting system is evaluated against baseline
models through controlled comparison and a structured ablation study. The research proceeds
through a structured pipeline: audio stems are  first separated using the Demucs source
separation model  [19];  spectral and  prosodic  features are independently  extracted and
processed by two dedicated branches; the branch outputs are fused through an attention-based
mechanism; and Bayesian uncertainty estimation is applied to produce calibrated confidence
scores at both the system level and the individual branch level.
(Note: The document references Figure 1 here, depicting the Methodological Framework of
Know-Ta!)
Data Collection
       This study uses two publicly available, open-access datasets released for research
purposes. The SONICS dataset [46], released alongside ICLR 2025, is used for the primary
training phase and contains 97,164 English-language tracks split near-evenly between 48,090
human-made songs and 49,074 AI-generated tracks sourced from Suno and Udio. The AIME
dataset  is used  exclusively  for cross-platform generalization testing and contains 12,000
English-language tracks, half human-made and half AI-generated, sourced from twelve different
AI platforms that were not used during the training phase. The use of two separate datasets with
non-overlapping AI platforms directly tests whether Know-Ta! can detect AI-generated music
from tools it has never encountered, which is the primary unresolved failure of existing detection
systems [24]. Both datasets contain exclusively English-language music, and this study's scope
is therefore limited to English-language track detection.
Data Preprocessing

All music files are standardized before training to ensure fair comparison across tracks.
Every song is resampled to 22,050 Hz and segmented into 30-second clips of uniform length,
with volume normalization applied to remove loudness differences across tracks. The SONICS
dataset  is partitioned into three subsets: 70% for model training, 10% for validation during
training, and 20% for internal testing. For the Audio Branch, each 30-second clip is converted
into a Mel-Spectrogram representation, producing a two-dimensional time-frequency image that
the EfficientNet-B0 network processes as visual input. For the Vocal Branch, the Demucs
source separation model [19]  is applied to each  clip to isolate the vocal stem from the
instrumental background before prosodic feature extraction is performed. This stem separation
step ensures that the Vocal Branch receives a clean, instrument-free signal, improving the
reliability of breathing pause detection, vibrato analysis, and pitch variation measurement.
Model Architecture Design

Audio Branch
      The Audio Branch employs EfficientNet-B0 [20], pre-trained on audio classification tasks
[21], a Convolutional Neural Network architecture designed using compound coefficient scaling
that simultaneously optimizes network width, depth, and resolution. This makes  it the most
parameter-efficient CNN architecture available, achieving high accuracy with significantly fewer
parameters than alternatives such as ResNet, VGG, or DenseNet [25]. A 2025 benchmark study
directly compared EfficientNet-B0 against VGG16, VGG19, ResNet50, DenseNet121, and
MobileNetV2 on Mel-Spectrograms for audio deepfake detection, confirming EfficientNet-B0 as
the strongest performer on this specific task [25]. The Audio Branch accepts Mel-Spectrogram
representations of the instrumental stem as input, treating them as two-dimensional images

from which the network learns harmonic, rhythmic, and timbral patterns. Mel-Spectrograms are
used as the input representation because they map audio frequencies onto the perceptual Mel
scale, mirroring how the human auditory system processes sound, and empirical comparisons
have shown that Mel-Spectrograms  significantly outperform other spectral representations
including MFCCs, CQT  chromagrams,  and  cyclic  tempograms  for CNN-based  audio
classification tasks [26]. The Audio Branch produces a 512-dimensional feature vector and an
independent Audio Confidence Score.
Vocal Branch
      The Vocal Branch uses Bidirectional Long Short-Term Memory networks to capture
temporal dependencies in vocal performance characteristics. Bidirectional LSTM was originally
proposed  for singing voice detection  specifically because vocal features such as vibrato,
breathing pauses, and pitch contours unfold across time in both directions, requiring both past
and future temporal context to be properly identified [27]. A standard unidirectional LSTM
processes only past context and  is structurally unable to capture these bidirectional vocal
patterns, making the bidirectional architecture theoretically necessary rather than optional for
this task. A direct comparison of LSTM, Bidirectional LSTM, and Transformer architectures on
audio deepfake detection confirmed that Bi-LSTM achieves the best Equal Error Rate at 0.43%
and the highest overall accuracy, outperforming both alternatives [28]. A 2025 Nature-published
study further validated that integrating prosodic features including pitch, temporal dynamics, and
glottal parameters into parallel LSTM-based modules significantly improves real-versus-fake
audio separability compared to spectral features alone [29].
      The Vocal Branch receives the isolated vocal stem produced by Demucs [19] and
extracts explicit prosodic features including breathing pause timing, vibrato rate and regularity,
pitch micro-variation, and voice energy dynamics. These features are grounded in established
detection research: the absence of regular human vocal biomarkers such as breathing pause
patterns, vibrato regularity, and pitch micro-variation has been demonstrated as a reliable and
peer-reviewed signal for distinguishing authentic human audio from machine-generated audio
[23]. AI systems have no biological equivalent to these constraints. The Vocal Branch produces
a 512-dimensional feature vector and an independent Vocal Confidence Score.
Attention-Based Fusion
      The  outputs  of  the Audio Branch and  Vocal Branch are combined through an
attention-based fusion mechanism. Introduced formally by Vaswani et al. [30], attention-based
weighting allows a model to learn which inputs deserve more weight based on the content of the
specific input being processed, optimized end-to-end through backpropagation. For Know-Ta!,
the fusion layer learns two parameters, alpha for the Audio Branch weight and beta for the Vocal
Branch weight, which adapt dynamically based on the content of the input track. This allows the
system to prioritize the Audio Branch for instrumental-heavy music and the Vocal Branch for
singing-heavy tracks without manual configuration.
Simple concatenation of branch outputs, also called early fusion, treats both branches as
equally important regardless of input content and has been empirically shown to underperform
attention-based fusion because it cannot suppress irrelevant information or emphasize the most
discriminative signal [32]. Multimodal learning theory further provides a mathematical guarantee
for  this design: the  utility function  for adding a complementary modality  is monotonically
non-decreasing, meaning combining two branches that capture different aspects of the same

problem can only maintain or improve performance compared to either branch alone [33]. This
theoretical guarantee is supported in practice by the 2025 SAFE International Audio Deepfake
Detection Challenge, where an attention-based gating mechanism that dynamically weighted
multiple expert detectors ranked first globally across all challenge tasks [31].
Bayesian Uncertainty Estimation
      Standard deep neural networks produce a single confident prediction even when the
input is genuinely ambiguous, which is a critical limitation in a music authentication context
where a wrongly confident false positive  directly harms a human  artist. To address  this,
Know-Ta! incorporates Monte Carlo Dropout [39] as a practical Bayesian approximation. During
inference, dropout layers remain active and the same input is passed through the model across
multiple forward passes. The mean of the resulting prediction distribution serves as the final
output, and  the variance  quantifies the model's  uncertainty. This approach  requires no
architectural changes to the existing EfficientNet-B0 or Bi-LSTM components and integrates
cleanly into the dual-branch pipeline.
Two types of uncertainty are reported following the framework established by Kendall and Gal
[40]:  aleatoric  uncertainty, which  reflects ambiguity inherent  in the input track  itself, and
epistemic uncertainty, which  reflects gaps in the model's training exposure. Distinguishing
between these types is important because a track that is genuinely borderline is a different
problem from a track the model has simply never encountered before. To ensure that the
reported  confidence  scores  are  meaningful and  trustworthy  rather  than  systematically
overconfident, Temperature Scaling [41] is applied as a post-training calibration step. Deep
Ensembles [42]  is identified as a stronger alternative uncertainty estimation strategy and is
recommended as a direction for future work, particularly for production-scale deployment where
computational cost is less constrained.
The system surfaces uncertainty at three levels: an overall Bayesian Confidence Score for the
final  prediction, a per-branch confidence score  for the Audio Branch and Vocal Branch
independently, and a conflict flag that is triggered when the two branches produce substantially
diverging verdicts. This directly addresses cases where the audio characteristics of a track
suggest AI generation while the vocal characteristics suggest human performance, or vice
versa, giving users a transparent and interpretable output rather than a binary label alone.
Baseline Comparison and Ablation Study
      To validate the contribution of each architectural component, Know-Ta! is evaluated
against five baseline configurations following the formal ablation methodology established by
Meyes et al. [34] and adopted in recent deepfake detection research [38]. Ablation studies are
necessary because while individual components are designed with specific purposes, the actual
contribution of each component to overall system performance cannot be claimed without
removing it and measuring the resulting change [35]. The six models evaluated are as follows:
Model 1 is an SVM classifier with MFCC features, representing the traditional machine learning
baseline that established Phase 1 of the detection field [37]. Model 2 is a Random Forest
classifier with spectral features, providing an ensemble baseline for interpretable feature-based
classification. Model 3 is the Audio Branch in isolation using EfficientNet-B0 only, which isolates
the contribution of spectral analysis. Model 4 is the Vocal Branch in isolation using Bi-LSTM
only, which isolates the contribution of prosodic analysis. Model 5 is a naive dual-branch system
using  simple  concatenation  fusion  without  the  attention mechanism, which  isolates the

contribution  of the attention-based  weighting. Model 6  is the  full Know-Ta! system with
dual-branch architecture, attention fusion, and Bayesian uncertainty estimation. This structure
directly mirrors the comparative logic used in recent CNN-BiLSTM hybrid deepfake detection
research, where  isolating each component before presenting the  full system result  is the
established standard for evidence-based architectural claims [36][38].
Performance Evaluation
      System performance  is evaluated using  six complementary metrics  following the
standardized benchmark protocol recommended by Deepfake-Eval-2024 [44], which identifies
selective single-metric reporting as a critical methodological flaw in prior detection literature.
Accuracy measures overall classification correctness across the test set. Precision quantifies
how many of the tracks flagged as AI-generated were actually AI-generated, which is critical
because a false positive means a human artist's real song is incorrectly labeled as AI, carrying
direct reputational and economic consequences. Recall quantifies how many of the truly
AI-generated tracks in the test set were successfully detected, which is critical because a false
negative allows  synthetic music  to pass undetected onto streaming platforms. F1-Score
provides the harmonic mean of Precision and Recall for balanced assessment when both error
types  carry  real-world  consequences  [43]. ROC-AUC  measures  threshold-independent
discriminative power, enabling  fair comparison with other systems that may use different
classification boundaries [45].
The sixth and most novel metric is the Cross-Platform Performance Drop Percentage, computed
as the difference between the F1-Score on the SONICS internal test set and the F1-Score on
the AIME  cross-platform  test  set.  This  metric  directly  quantifies how much  detection
performance degrades when the system encounters AI platforms  it has never seen before,
which  is the primary unresolved failure of all existing music detectors [24]. No prior music
detection paper has reported  this  metric  explicitly, and  its inclusion  is a methodological
contribution of this study.
System Deployment
      Know-Ta!  is  deployed  as  a web  application  that  allows  users  to  upload an
English-language music file in MP3 or WAV format and receive a real-time authenticity analysis
without requiring any technical expertise. The web interface presents the overall prediction of
Real or AI, the Bayesian Confidence Score as a percentage, the independent Audio Branch and
Vocal Branch confidence scores, a conflict flag when the two branches produce diverging
verdicts, and a plain-language explanation of the specific indicators that contributed to the
detection  result, such as  irregular breathing patterns or mechanically regular vibrato. The
trained model is saved and loaded at inference time so that no retraining is required for each
new analysis. The web deployment directly addresses the accessibility gap identified in the
significance of  this study: music  listeners, independent  artists, and platforms with limited
resources  for content  verification gain access to a practical and transparent authenticity
verification tool without requiring specialized software or hardware.
